title: Automated 3D planning of high tibial osteotomies optimised for specific morphotypes of the knee (smartHTO)
summary:
High tibial osteotomy (HTO) is a relevant treatment option for unicompartmental medial knee osteoarthritis (joint degeneration on the inner side of the knee joint) associated with a varus leg axis (so-called bowleg). HTO enables the correction of congenital or post-traumatic deformities (alterations resulting from accidents). Additionally, HTO can serve as a protective procedure for cartilage regenerative interventions, such as autologous chondrocyte implantation, as well as following severe meniscal damage (e.g., after partial medial meniscectomy).
The objective of the correction is to shift the loads into the physiological (normal) range of neighboring joint compartments, thereby slowing the progression of osteoarthritis. In contrast to joint replacement techniques such as unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA / partial knee replacement) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA / total knee replacement), HTO preserves the patient's native joint. Furthermore, compared to UKA, HTO has been reported to yield a higher postoperative range of motion and a superior level of physical activity (Fu et al. 2013; Cao et al. 2018; Screpis et al. 2023). Consequently, HTO can prevent or delay the necessity of joint replacement while providing the advantage of superior knee functionality. Particularly for younger patients who tend to maintain higher activity levels and thus place greater demands on knee joint function, HTO represents a viable alternative to UKA or TKA. A subsequent conversion to a knee prosthesis remains fully possible at any time.
Despite these significant advantages of HTO compared to UKA and TKA, and notwithstanding long-standing experience with this surgical procedure, success rates of HTO vary. Up to 16% of patients require conversion to a UKA or TKA within 5 years after the intervention (Keenan et al. 2019; Ollivier et al. 2021), which represents an insufficient delay of joint-sacrificing surgery.
Regularly, this operation is planned using standardized, conventional, two-dimensional (2D) radiographs. Due to methodological limitations, this can lead to inaccuracies in surgical planning. Within the framework of our scientific study, we aim to optimize this planning process by utilizing additional state-of-the-art 3D technology and biomechanical computer simulations. In the further course of the project, we aim to automate these elaborate manual planning processes. Through the use of CT data, we aspire to achieve a more specific planning of your postoperative patellar height, the spatial relationships between the patella and the tibia, as well as the overall impact on knee joint mobility, while explicitly taking soft-tissue structures into account (e.g., anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, medial and lateral collateral ligaments of the knee joint).

The primary objectives of this study are to evaluate:
• how the new technique affects your knee function,
• the level of patient satisfaction following surgery,
• how the enhanced planning process influences surgical outcomes,
• the correlation between preoperative planning and postoperative analysis/results.

The findings of this study are intended to help further optimize the surgical care of future patients.

interventions.name: Patients with unicompartmental medial knee osteoarthritis associated with a varus leg axis will undergo open-wedge high tibial osteotomy (owHTO) and will be followed up for 24 months

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients undergoing proximal tibial valgization osteotomy at the Department of Sports Traumatology, BG Trauma Center Murnau.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients under 18 years of age
